children: By Paulo Trevisani and Emese Bartha
The global bond selloff took a breather Thursday and borrowing costs fell to just below multidecade highs, amid bets that U.S. interest rates may not rise as fast as previously thought.
The 10-year Treasury yield slipped to 5.213% after reaching a 24-year high of 5.338% overnight. The two-year yield declined to 4.765% from 4.856%.
Fresh data indicated that the economy remains hot but isn't accelerating too much. That looked enough to trigger bond buying in a market that might have been oversold.
"We should be clear that positioning and positioning of shorts has been very one-directional and near extremes," said George Catrambone, head of fixed income Americas at DWS.
Catrambone said that many of the forces driving the selloff remain in place and yields remain elevated. High yields, in turn, would eventually slow down the economy and retreat to lower levels.

"No one is suggesting that we're going to ride this all the way back down to 3.5% again on the front end," he said. "I'm just saying, you know, overall, this is certainly ratcheting up tightness in certain segments of the economy."

Thursday's yield decline may reflect investors unwinding bets that bond prices, which move in opposite direction of yields, would fall ahead of the U.S. employment report to be released Friday, said John Briggs, head of U.S. rates strategy at Natixis.

Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal expect a slowdown in job creation, which could support the case for a slower pace of interest rate increases by the Fed. Odds of a hold this month ticked higher to 70% from 62% yesterday, according to CME.
The U.S. yield drop was also influenced by moves in Europe, where the 10-year German Bund yield fell to 3.529% from 3.637% as safety-seeking investors fled markets deemed less stable, Briggs said.
"[I]t turned in Europe to everything selling off to periphery and France causing a flight to quality to Germany."

European investors also are watching French government bonds, where budget concerns weigh on investors' confidence, pushing the spread between 10-year French and German government bond yields as high as 133 basis points, a 14-year high, before retreating to 128 basis points.
Meanwhile, investors are assessing whether high yields make bonds attractive or whether the risk of yields rising further is too great.
Long-dated Treasury yield levels above 5% are both a warning and an opportunity, said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial.
"Existing bondholders have absorbed painful price declines, but new capital can now lock in yields unavailable for much of the past two decades," he said.
